To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) mTOR inhibitor can induce differentiation of a neuroblastoma cell into osteoblastic cell without an intermediate stem cell step; 2) mTOR inhibitor induce metabolic changes that can be used to identify a differentiated cell; 3) mTOR inhibitor induces morphological changes in a neuroblastoma cells that can be used as a marker of differentiation.
the mTOR inhibitor rapamycin is able to induce differentiation of human neuroblastomas cells toward the osteoblastic lineage.

the differentiation of cancer cells into a different germ layer lineage can be induced by the modulation of few molecules, such as mTOR, and that the presence of a specific extracellular matrix (ECM) is crucial to the differentiation of cancer stem cells (cSCs) toward different lineages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular mechanisms that regulate the differentiation of neoplastic cells, and their potential application in the development of new therapies.

the possibility to differentiate a tumor cell into a normal cell by a metabolic and genetic reprogramming, and to use these cells to generate functional tissues for tissue engineering and regenerative medicine.

the identification of the mechanisms involved in the control of the differentiation of a cancer cell and the possibility of using the differentiation process to control the tumor growth and progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(1) the differentiation of a cell toward a specific germ layer is a complex phenomenon that is regulated by the interaction among different factors; (2) the differentiation process is not necessarily a stepwise one, and it is possible to obtain the differentiation of a neoplastic cells directly into a specific cell lineage; (3) the differentiation of cancer cells toward a specific lineage could be a possible strategy to obtain a 'normalization' of these cells and to obtain their elimination.
the cell fate can be controlled directly from a cancer cell by modulating few key factors, which in turn are able to control the metabolic and functional changes.
the cell fate is controlled by a network of master molecules that can be modulated by the environment and the metabolic changes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the differentiation process of neuroblastoma cells is not a linear pathway but it can be driven toward multiple lineages, by different stimuli.
a neoplastic cancer cell is not a terminally differentiated cell, but a 'frozen' cell, which can be pushed to differentiate toward different lineages, depending on its microenvironment.

1) a cancer stem cell is not a necessary step to obtain a differentiated cell, 2) the metabolic changes observed in cancer stem cells are not a consequence of the differentiation process but they are the cause, 3) the scaffold presence is not a prerequisite to differentiate a cancer cell, and 4) the master molecule is not the only determinant of cell fate.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a cancer stem cell population is not necessary for the differentiation of neoplastic cells toward the different lineages, but the metabolic and epigenetic status of the cell is the most important determinant in this process.

the differentiation of cancer cells is not a simple process, but it is the result of a complex interaction among several factors, including the scaffold, the cell metabolism and the expression of master molecules.
a neoplastic stem cell is not necessary to trigger the tumor growth, and that a differentiated cancer cell can be induced to differentiate toward a specific lineage.
